description: We are a passionate team of Computer Science students working on innovative AI and software solutions for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. Our stack includes Web Development, AI/Machine Learning, and Problem Solving. We are dedicated to building a creative, high-impact project.
summary:
AstroPulse is an autonomous astronaut health monitoring platform developed by Team AstroNode for deep-space missions such as Artemis IV. Because communication delays of up to 22 minutes and solar conjunction blackouts prevent real-time Earth medical support, crews need onboard clinical autonomy during acute emergencies.

AstroPulse provides a real-time medical HUD that tracks crew physiological vitals (heart rate, SpO2, core temperature, and stress) alongside cabin conditions (CO2, pressure, and radiation). Instead of acting as a passive dashboard, it pairs anomaly detection with closed-loop countermeasures—guiding crew members through immediate corrective actions and verifying physiological recovery. It features dual views for the Flight Surgeon and individual astronauts, isolates communication dropouts from false clinical alerts, and integrates AURA, a Gemini-powered AI assistant with an offline fallback engine. Built with React, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS, this prototype simulates telemetry calibrated to NASA HRP and ECLSS standards.
details:
When our team (Team AstroNode) started looking into deep-space missions like Artemis IV, one question kept coming back to us: what happens when an astronaut gets into medical trouble millions of kilometers away from Earth, and the radio takes 22 minutes just to say "help"?

In Low Earth Orbit, flight surgeons on the ground are practically in the room with the crew. Beyond the Moon and on the way to Mars, that safety net disappears. That realization became the heart of AstroPulse—an onboard medical companion and health monitoring HUD built to give crews real medical autonomy when Earth is out of reach.

How AstroPulse Works Instead of building another passive screen full of blinking numbers, we wanted a system that thinks alongside the crew under pressure. AstroPulse tracks core physiological vitals (heart rate, SpO2, core temperature, and stress) right next to spacecraft cabin conditions (CO2 levels, pressure, and radiation), calibrated to NASA HRP and ECLSS baselines. When an emergency hits—like a CO2 scrubber failure or a sudden solar flare—AstroPulse doesn't just sound an alarm. It connects the alert to closed-loop countermeasures, guiding the crew through the exact corrective action and watching their vitals recover in real time.

What We Cared About Most (Human Factors & Design) Every design choice came from putting ourselves in the crew's boots during a high-stress emergency:

  • No False Panic During Blackouts: Deep-space links drop all the time. We made sure a lost radio signal never triggers a fake medical emergency on a healthy astronaut.
  • Respecting Privacy & Roles: A Flight Surgeon needs to triage the whole crew at a glance, while an individual astronaut just wants a calm, private space to check their own health and talk through stress. We built tailored views for both.
  • AURA—Always There, Even Offline: We integrated Google's Gemini AI into our assistant, AURA, so crew members can ask natural questions about their health. Because space missions lose connectivity, we also engineered a deterministic offline brain so AURA never goes silent when the internet or ground link drops.
  • Calm Under Pressure: We designed a clean 3-column HUD with low-glare space themes (Deep Space, Nebula, and NASA Tactical) and alert filtering so the crew never suffers from alarm fatigue.

How We Built It We built AstroPulse from the ground up using React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and Zustand, backed by a custom physiological-environmental simulation engine, automated tests with Vitest, and Google Gemini API. Our open-source repository is available on GitHub :[https://github.com/Ganat1337/nasa-health-monitoring-final](https://github.com/Ganat1337/nasa-health-monitoring-final)

and deployed live on Vercel ([https://nasa-health-monitoring-final.vercel.app](https://nasa-health-monitoring-final.vercel.app)).

Intended Impact Our hope with AstroPulse is simple: as humanity pushes farther into deep space, technology shouldn't just collect data—it should stand beside the crew as a calm, reliable medical partner when they are truly on their own.
